title: The Atlantic revolutions
note: Between 1775 and 1825, revolutions swept the Atlantic world. Inspired by Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and popular sovereignty, Americans, French, Haitians and Latin Americans overthrew colonial or royal rule. Each revolution also raised the question of who counted as a citizen.

read.title: An age of revolution
text: In 1775 thirteen British colonies in North America took up arms against new taxes and laws passed without their consent. With French help, they won independence in 1783. Their success, and the language of natural rights in their Declaration of Independence, inspired others.

France was next. Deeply in debt, Louis XVI summoned the Estates-General in 1789. The Third Estate, representing commoners, declared itself a National Assembly, and Parisians stormed the Bastille. The Assembly abolished noble privileges and proclaimed the Rights of Man. As war and fear of counterrevolution grew, radicals executed the king in 1793 and launched the Reign of Terror. Exhausted by turmoil, France accepted the rule of Napoleon Bonaparte, who kept some revolutionary reforms in his law code but crowned himself emperor.

In Saint-Domingue, France's richest colony, enslaved people rose up in 1791. Led by Toussaint Louverture and then Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they defeated French, British and Spanish forces and founded Haiti in 1804, the first nation born of a successful slave revolt.

When Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808, Spain's American colonies began to govern themselves. Creole leaders such as Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led armies of independence, and by the mid-1820s nearly all of Spanish and Portuguese America was free of European rule.
